# Education in Finland: Key Features and Structure
Education in Finland is characterized by universal access, high quality, and a strong emphasis on equality. The system begins with non-mandatory early childhood education, including daycare and preschool/kindergarten, available to all children from eight months to six years, focusing on the development of social skills and readiness to learn. Basic education is compulsory from ages 7 to 18 and consists of a nine-year comprehensive school taught by highly qualified teachers, all of whom must hold a master's degree. The curriculum includes arts, languages, and practical subjects, with small class sizes and a relaxed, child-centered learning environment. Students receive free health services, daily lunch, all learning materials, and transportation if needed. The use of tuition fees in basic education is prohibited, and grading is based on mastery rather than high-stakes testing.
After basic school, students choose between academic upper secondary school (lukio) or vocational school (ammattioppilaitos), both tuition-free and now compulsory until the age of 18. Academic upper secondary culminates in a national matriculation exam, while vocational tracks offer professional certification and pathways to higher education. Tertiary education is provided by research universities and universities of applied sciences (AMKs), with admission strictly based on merit—GPA, matriculation exam results, and entrance exams. Tuition is free for EU/EEA students; non-EU/EEA students pay fees. Finland values continuous adult education and supports it through municipal adult education centers and open university programs. The system emphasizes multilingualism, offering at least two additional languages beyond the native tongue. Finnish education is governed primarily by local municipalities, with minimal private schooling. Internationally, Finland operates official curriculum schools abroad and exports Finnish-style education through initiatives such as the Education Finland programme.
